subject: Mathematics
title: Sets and Functions
learningOutcomes: Describe mathematics as the study of patterns, structure and relationships, and continue number patterns including the Fibonacci sequence.
Identify sets, subsets, overlapping and disjoint sets, and apply operations on two and three sets using Venn diagrams.
Solve classification and cataloguing problems on two and three sets using Venn diagrams and the inclusion-exclusion formula.
Verify and apply the commutative, associative and distributive laws and De Morgan's laws for three sets.
Apply set theory to real-world problems such as demographic classification and categorizing products in a shopping mall.
Explain the Cartesian product and binary relations with their domain and range.
Represent a relation by a table, by ordered pairs and by a graph.
Use function notation to find the value, domain and range of a function.
Identify into, onto, one-one (injective), surjective and bijective functions using mapping diagrams.

sections.heading: Patterns and the Fibonacci sequence
sections.body: Mathematics studies patterns, structure and relationships. A pattern may add a fixed number each time, e.g. \(2,5,8,11,\dots\). In the Fibonacci sequence each term is the sum of the two terms before it: \(F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}\), giving \(1,1,2,3,5,8,\dots\).

sections.heading: Sets and their kinds
sections.body: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. It is written in tabular form \(\{1,2,3\}\) or set-builder form \(\{x\mid x\in\mathbb{N},\ x\lt 4\}\). Kinds of sets: empty \(\varnothing\), singleton, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent and universal \(U\). \(\mathbb{N}\subset\mathbb{W}\subset\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathbb{Q}\cup\mathbb{Q}'=\mathbb{R}\).

sections.heading: Subsets and power set
sections.body: \(A\subseteq B\) means every element of A is in B; \(A\subset B\) means a proper subset. The power set \(P(S)\) is the set of all subsets of S. If \(n(S)=m\) then \(n\{P(S)\}=2^{m}\) and S has \(2^{m}-1\) proper subsets.

sections.heading: Operations on sets
sections.body: Union \(A\cup B\) (in A or B), intersection \(A\cap B\) (in both), difference \(A-B\) (in A but not B) and complement \(A'=U-A\). Disjoint sets have \(A\cap B=\varnothing\); overlapping sets share some elements but neither is a subset of the other.

sections.heading: Laws of sets
sections.body: Commutative: \(A\cup B=B\cup A\). Associative: \(A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\). Distributive: \(A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)\). De Morgan: \((A\cup B)'=A'\cap B'\) and \((A\cap B)'=A'\cup B'\).

sections.heading: Venn diagrams and counting
sections.body: \(n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)\). For three sets: \(n(A\cup B\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\cap B)-n(A\cap C)-n(B\cap C)+n(A\cap B\cap C)\). Fill a three-set Venn diagram from the centre outwards.

sections.heading: Relations
sections.body: An ordered pair \((x,y)\) has an abscissa x and an ordinate y. The Cartesian product \(A\times B\) is the set of all ordered pairs with first element from A and second from B; \(n(A\times B)=n(A)\cdot n(B)\). A relation is any subset of \(A\times B\); its domain is the set of first elements and its range the set of second elements.

sections.heading: Functions and their types
sections.body: A function \(f:A\to B\) is a relation in which every element of A has exactly one image in B. Domain = A, co-domain = B, range = set of images. One-one: different inputs, different outputs. Onto: range = co-domain. Into: range is smaller than the co-domain. Bijective: one-one and onto. Linear: \(y=mx+c\); quadratic: \(y=ax^{2}+bx+c\).

definitions.definition: A well-defined collection of distinct objects.
The set of all subsets of S, written \(P(S)\); it has \(2^{m}\) elements when \(n(S)=m\).
Sets with no common element: \(A\cap B=\varnothing\).
\(A\times B\) = all ordered pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\).
Any subset of \(A\times B\), a set of ordered pairs.
A relation in which each element of the domain has exactly one image.
A function whose range equals its co-domain.
A function that is both one-one and onto.

examTips: In inclusion-exclusion problems, always subtract the overlap once: \(n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)\).
For three-set Venn problems start with the centre region \(A\cap B\cap C\) and work outwards by subtraction.
To check a function, list the first elements: none may repeat and every element of the domain must appear.
Do not forget the empty set and the set itself when counting subsets: \(2^{m}\) in all.
